title: Blocking cotton crochet
subtitle: How to wet-block or steam-block cotton for a flat, even finish
excerpt: Cotton responds well to both wet blocking and steam. A blocked piece lies flat and shows stitch definition clearly, and holds its shape through washing.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: The process of wetting or steaming a finished piece and shaping it to measurements while damp or under heat, so it dries or cools in the correct dimensions.
A blocking method that involves soaking or spraying the piece with water, pinning it to shape, and leaving it to dry.

aliases: how to block cotton yarn crochet

content.text: Cotton absorbs water readily and relaxes when wet, which makes
the standard method for cotton crochet.
evens out tension differences and helps flat squares lie without curling. It also opens lace motifs fully. Most cotton pieces benefit from blocking before seaming.
Submerge the piece in cool water for 15 to 20 minutes until fully saturated.
Gently squeeze out water. Do not wring or twist. Roll in a clean towel and press to remove more water.
Lay the piece on a blocking mat. Pin corners first to the required measurements, then pin edges in sections, easing the fabric to size.
For lace, pin every point or picot to open the pattern fully.
Leave until completely dry, at least several hours or overnight. Do not unpin until dry.

For pieces that are close to correct but need minor shaping, spray blocking is faster than full immersion. Pin the piece to shape, then mist evenly with a spray bottle until damp (not soaked). Pat flat and leave to dry pinned.

Steam also works on cotton and is faster than wet blocking. Pin the piece dry to the required measurements, hold a steam iron 5 to 10 cm above the surface, and move it slowly over the fabric. Do not press down. Let the piece cool and dry fully before unpinning.

items.symptom: The piece curled back to its original shape after drying
items.cause: It was unpinned before fully dry, or the yarn has a high twist that resists blocking.
items.fix: Leave pins in until completely dry. Re-wet if needed. For very stiff cotton, a light starch spray can help hold the shape.

items.symptom: The fabric puckered around the pin sites
items.cause: The pins were too far apart, creating tension between pinning points.
items.fix: Add more pins between existing ones and re-pin with smaller gaps between each point.

items.cause: The dye was not fixed properly or the yarn was labelled as pre-washed when it was not.
items.fix: Rinse in cool water until the water runs clear. Add a small amount of white vinegar to the final rinse to help fix loose dye.

content.text: Block a granny square after making one and compare it to an unblocked square from the same batch. The difference in how flat and even it lies shows why blocking is worth doing before assembling a joined project.
